pll1d39c1-d1e3501.summary: Raises the question whether God's knowledge can increase or decrease, since both seem provable.

pll1d39c1-d1e3504.summary: Argues it can change: someone who will not read today can read today, and whatever can happen can be known by God, so God can know what he does not know; conversely he can fail to know what he knows, so his knowledge can increase or decrease.

pll1d39c1-d1e3507.summary: Answers that God's knowledge is wholly immutable and can neither increase nor decrease.

pll1d39c1-d1e3511.summary: Cites De Trinitate XV: God's knowledge is his wisdom, and his wisdom his essence, since in his wonderful simplicity to be wise is to be.

pll1d39c1-d1e3530.summary: Continues Augustine: the Word knows all the Father knows, receiving knowing from the Father as he receives being, since knowing and being are one there. The Father, as it were speaking himself, begot a Word equal in all; Father and Son know each other, one by begetting, the other by being born. Each sees all things in their knowledge, wisdom, and essence at once, not piecemeal or alternately.
claims: The Word receives knowing as he receives being.
The Word is equal to the Father in all.

pll1d39c1-d1e3544.summary: Concludes that God's knowledge is as invariable as his essence, and Father, Son, and Spirit know and see all at once. Yet it is granted that God can know what he does not know and not know what he knows, since something could be subject to his knowledge that is not, or not be that is, without change in the knowledge.
claims: God can know otherwise only by difference in objects, not in knowledge.

pl-l1d39c1.summary: Asks whether God's knowledge can increase or decrease. It seems so: God can know that someone who will not read today reads, so he can know what he does not know; and he can fail to know what he knows. Lombard holds God's knowledge wholly immutable: with Augustine, God's knowledge is his wisdom and essence, since in his simplicity to know is to be. The Word knows all the Father knows, receiving knowing as he receives being; Father and Son know each other and see all things at once, not successively. Yet God can know what he does not know and not know what he knows, because something could be or not be subject to his knowledge without change in the knowledge itself.
claims: God's knowledge is wholly immutable and cannot increase or decrease.
God's knowledge is his wisdom and essence.
In God, to know is to be.
The Son knows all the Father knows, receiving knowing from the Father as he receives being.
God sees all things at once, not successively.
God can know what he does not know, since objects could differ without change in his knowledge.
